result:
The first thing that comes is the quiet hum of an empty house at 3:17 a.m. and the way the refrigerator clicks on like it’s clearing its throat. I’m sitting here with the screen glowing against my face, 1000 words to spend like loose change, and suddenly every trivial memory feels urgent.

I remember the summer I was nine and my grandfather taught me how to sharpen a pocket knife on a whetstone. He’d spit on the stone first, a small personal sacrament, then draw the blade across it with the solemn patience of a man who’d already outlived two wars and one wife. The sound was like a secret being told. When I finally got it sharp enough to shave the hair off my arm, he looked at me with something between pride and pity and said, “Now you know how easy it is to take things apart. The hard part is knowing when not to.” I lost that knife in a lake two weeks later and never told him. Some lessons you only half-learn on purpose.

There’s a peculiar grief that comes with realizing your childhood heroes were just tired people trying their best. My mother could make a pot of soup last a week and still have it taste like mercy. She’d stand at the stove stirring with one hand while grading papers with the other, red pen moving like a tired bird. I thought she was magic. Later I understood she was simply stubborn and in love with us in the way that love sometimes looks like exhaustion wearing an apron.

I keep thinking about how we’re all just soft animals wearing clothes, pretending we’re not terrified of the dark that lives inside our own skulls. We build cathedrals out of small talk. We say “how are you” when what we mean is “please don’t leave me alone with myself today.” We doomscroll through other people’s curated pain looking for proof that we’re not the only ones quietly unraveling.

There’s a Japanese concept called *kintsugi*—the art of repairing broken pottery with gold. The cracks aren’t hidden; they’re illuminated. I’ve been trying to live like that. Every panic attack, every stupid mistake, every time I said the cruel thing because I was scared—these are the gold lines now. They make the vessel stronger and more interesting. The bowl that has never been broken can only ever be a bowl. The one that’s been shattered and remade knows what it costs to hold anything at all.

I’ve been in love exactly three and a half times. The half was a woman who kissed like she was trying to memorize the exact shape of regret. We lasted eleven days and I still think about her when it rains in a certain way. The others were bigger, messier, more instructive. Love, I’ve learned, is mostly the willingness to keep choosing someone after you’ve seen the rough draft of their soul. It’s saying “I see the monster and the child and the person trying so hard” and still reaching for their hand in the dark.

Sometimes I worry I’m becoming the kind of person who collects beautiful sentences instead of actually living. I read too much. Feel too much. Translate everything into language like some desperate cartographer trying to map the territory of being alive. But language fails in the places that matter most. There is no word for the sound your mother makes when she laughs at her own joke. No adequate description for how it feels when someone remembers how you take your coffee after six months apart. The heart is stubbornly analog in a digital world.

I want to tell you about the time I drove through Nevada at night with the windows down and the radio playing songs I didn’t even like anymore. The desert was so dark it felt like driving through God’s ribcage. Every once in a while headlights would appear like distant ships and we’d pass each other with that brief, sacred recognition of two humans hurtling through emptiness at 80 miles an hour. For a moment I understood everything. Then the moment passed and I was just a guy who needed to pee again.

The older I get, the more I suspect that the point was never to figure it all out. The point was to stay soft enough that the world could still surprise you. To keep being stupidly sincere in an age that rewards clever detachment. To cry at commercials sometimes and mean it when you say “I love you” and tip too much because the waitress looked tired.

There are 312 words left and I’m thinking about my friend who died last year. He used to send me voice memos at 2 a.m. that were just him breathing quietly before saying “You there, man?” like he needed to make sure the universe hadn’t ended while he wasn’t looking. I keep those messages. Sometimes I play them when the house gets too quiet. His voice is still warm. The universe, it turns out, keeps ending and beginning in small ways every single day.

I don’t know what this is. A confession? A love letter to being alive? Just words spilling out because you gave me permission and the cursor was blinking like a heartbeat?

Maybe that’s all any of us are doing. Bleeding language onto screens and pages and each other’s shoulders, trying to prove we were here. That we noticed the light on the water. That we loved badly and bravely. That we were stupid and magnificent and terrified and grateful in equal measure.

The refrigerator just clicked off. The house is holding its breath again.

I have 47 words left and I want to use every single one to say thank you. Thank you for the small mercies. For the songs that know your name. For the way dogs look at you like you personally invented morning. For the fact that you’re still trying even when it’s hard. For reading this far.

We’re all just stories telling stories to other stories, trying to remember what it felt like before we learned how to be afraid.

The last word is yours.

(Exactly 1000)
